items.text: Group schemes over a field: separable implies smooth

Theorem. $G$ a group scheme over a field $k$. The following are equivalent: $G$ is separable (geometrically reduced) over $k$; $G$ is geometrically normal over $k$; and, if $G$ is locally of finite type, $G$ is smooth over $k$.
The implications from smooth/normal to separable are trivial. Proof that separable $\Rightarrow$ geometrically normal: it suffices to show $G$ normal (after base change).
$x$ a maximal point: $\mathcal O_{G,x}$ is a field, separable over $k$, so $G$ is geometrically normal at $x$.
Take $k'\supset\kappa(x)$: a point $x'\in G'(k')$ above $x$ with $G'$ normal at $x'$.

For another $x'_1\in G'(k')$, left translation by $x'_1x'^{-1}$ is an automorphism of $G'$ over $k'$ carrying $x'$ to $x'_1$: $G'$ is normal at every $k'$-rational point (and likewise over any $k''\supset k'$).
Any $y\in G$ lifts to a rational point $y''\in G''$ for $k''\supset\kappa(y),k'$; $G''$ normal at $y''$, and normality descends: $G$ normal at $y$.
Same for smoothness: the argument uses only that the property descends and is invariant under isomorphism (homogeneity).
If $X$ is separable over $k$, then $X$ is geometrically normal; if moreover locally of finite type, $X$ is smooth.
$k$ perfect: $G_{\mathrm{red}}$ is a subgroup scheme, geometrically normal, and smooth if $G$ is locally of finite type.
Corollary. $G$ locally of finite type over a field: the connected components of $G$ are its irreducible components.

Proof. Pass to the perfect closure (homeomorphic); replace $G$ by $G_{\mathrm{red}}$ (same space). Then $G$ is geometrically normal, so its local rings are domains: through each point passes only one irreducible component, hence connected = irreducible components (locally noetherian spaces).
